lanes.label: Out of Carnia, for work
lanes.statusNote: the route is documented, the descent is not
nodes: A De Franceschi of Mione on the headmen's list, working in the County of Pazin. The roster also holds eight people of the name at Paluzza, one valley east in the same Carnia — unworked, and the nearest thing this archive has to a second door into the Val di Gorto

The County of Pazin itself — Pisino, the Habsburg island inside Venetian Istria and the jurisdiction the 1679 Mione man was working in. Kobler has a Giovanni Battista reaching Fiume from this county «intorno al 1740»; the town's own books run from 1582 and have never been opened here. One accepted record sits at Pisino on no lane at all
The surname enters the Moncalvo di Pisino baptism book
ANNO · DOMNI · 1711 cut over the door of the house

nodes.why: Joannes Baptista, farmer of house 5 — the line's earliest dated ancestor

nodes: Named in this line's own route description for a year before it was ever drawn on it: ten register entries, eight of them accepted, and twenty-one more people on the roster. Parenzo is where the inland parishes reach the western coast.
The stonecutter's son comes down to the coast between 1892 and 1894
ends: Antonio's brother's line, up the coast. Nine graves in the town cemetery and a shipping family — the same Carnian stock as Crikvenica, one headland further north.
Ivan, born Crikvenica 1925, taken to work in the Reich and issued papers at Pfullingen in Württemberg. The line's hinge: everything after 1945 leaves from here.
The post-war emigration out of Yugoslavia, and the one destination where the surname is still spelt three different ways inside one family.
Johannesburg. Thirteen of the seventeen people on earth who spell it «Defranceski» are here — an English clerk's spelling that became the family's own.
Two separate arrivals: the Eleven of Gračišće sending Basilio to Jackson Heights, and the older Istrian emigration to the mines.

Rotilio, eighth of the Eleven, is said to have gone to Buenos Aires with two daughters. Searched in September 2026 and not found — and the album’s one supporting detail, his wife’s name, turns out to be his sister’s marriage. The register has him at Gračišće, marrying, in 1928. Weaker than it was.

lanes.label: Svetvinčenat — the castle the name never left
nodes: The parish's real first page. «Alì 21 Decembre / Elena fiola di Fran.co de Franceschi» — the earliest entry of the name in this parish, and two sweeps had already read past it
«M.ro Nadal de Franceschi» and «M.ro Batta de Franceschi» baptising six weeks apart, both styled Maestro, and the godparents around them are the Carnian colony. Artisan, and rising
Eight years on the same register calls one of them «il Signor» — the same family, a different word

Four households of the name baptising at the castle at once — Jacobo × Pascasia, Matteo × Francisca, Pietro × Jacoba and Vittorio × Dominica, with Gasparo × Maria beside them. Jacobo × Pascasia, Matteo × Francisca, Pietro × Jacoba, Vittorio × Dominica, with Gasparo × Maria beside them. Read frame by frame through the fifteen years no index reaches; none of them is in any index anywhere
The daughters marry out. Elena to a Santalezza of the Albona territory, Fusca to a Jacomini of Parenzo — and a Corva «dà Cargna» marrying in. The sons stayed
The last leaf the filmed baptism books reach. Where the filmed baptism books stop. The marriages run on to 1858 and the deaths to 1917, both unread
ends: The castle was the head of that line until 28 September 2026. Whether the southern-Istrian group descends from these households, or they are a separate stock of the name, is the open question this archive split the lines apart to stop answering by accident. ⭐ The southern-Istria lane's own first node IS Svetvinčenat, 1628 — so the two are already drawn touching; what is NOT drawn, because it is not known, is descent.

lanes.label: Out of southern Istria — origin unknown
lanes.statusNote: at Ližnjan from 1815 · origin still not found
nodes: Sixty-three indexed entries between 1659 and 1894 and twenty-three volumes of parish book from 1613, and until today this town was on no lane on this chart. Carlo's book names Franceschi among the noble families of Pola «venuti da Capodistria» before the plague of 1631. The register writes it as both «Pola» and «Pula», which is why it went missing twice

Forty-two records and not one of them another family — a cleaner return than any Istrian parish but Ližnjan. Two households: Vittorio × Stella Tamborin and Giuseppe × Giovanna Beluzzi. Natale Mattio, Elisabetta and Irene, whom this archive listed under Pula, are all baptised here
A Maria Defranceski at Premantura, and again in 1859
Two born here who died in France

nodes.why: ⭐⭐⭐ CORRECTED 12 October 2026 — **this node said 1931 and it was out by 116 years.** *The old note was right that 1931 was a death year and not a Ližnjan date; what nobody had done was open the parish's own books.* **Ližnjan «Liber Copulatorum», page 1, entry 2 — the second marriage the book ever records:** «12 Novembre **1815**», house 17, «**Mario de Franceschi deto Marulin di Antonio**», aged **21**, *celibes*, to «Maddalena Percouich di Antonio». *He was born about 1794 and his father was Antonio.* **He died in the same house in 1839** — «Mattio Franceschi **d.to Marulin**, agr., ann. 40» — *with the byname written on him a second time, in a different book and a different hand.* **Three generations now stand in a row from these books:** Antonio → Mattio detto Marulin (m. 1815, d. 1839) → Antonius (b. 1819, m. 1861). *Eleven people of the name are in the burial register alone.*

ends: Grga died here, and thirteen graves of the name are in the city's cemeteries — the largest single concentration in Croatia.

A line drawn on a map years ago from Ližnjan to Monheim, with no note, no date and no name. Corrected in September 2026: the coordinates point at Bavaria, but the town that matters is Monheim am Rhein — and the only private listing of «Defranceski» in the whole German directory is five kilometres away at Langenfeld. Still lore. No longer sourceless.
Southern-Istrian emigration, separate from the Gračišće one and never yet joined to it.
Two born at Barban in 1924 who died in France — the clearest documented exit from this cluster.

lanes.label: Out of Venice, as soldiers
lanes.statusNote: a family chart reaches back to 1318
nodes: Louis I grants «nobiles regni Croacie»; the family is at Zadar from the 14th century
Francesco the Venetian lays the foundations of his house on 18 June 1584
Zuane takes the town and is paid in ruined land on the Vrljika
The mills: six wheels, then eleven, then fourteen
ends: The spring at the head of the Vrljika, and the mills the Republic paid Zuane with in 1717. Franceschi property into living memory.
Where the Dalmatian family is today, the particle stripped off by Napoleonic decree — which is why the descendants of a count are called Franceschi.

lanes.label: Out of Crete, as refugees
lanes.statusNote: the flight of 1669 is tradition, well supported
nodes: Nicolò castellan of Castel Milopotamo; the family noble in Crete

⚠ **CORRECTED 12 October 2026.** *This node read* «the fleet is wrecked in a storm» *and the lane called it documented.* ***Five sources on the evacuation were read and not one mentions a wreck.*** *The contemporary relation of the Grand Master of Malta describes the opposite — a negotiated embarkation over* **22 days**, *the Grand Vizier granting extensions and offering to forward the luggage;* **about 12,000 people left Candia**. *Morosini surrendered on 5 September 1669, without the Senate's authorisation, and* ***had already decided the refugees would be settled in the uninhabited places of the Adriatic*** — *which is how this family reached this coast.* ⚠ *The wreck may be family tradition, or a slide from the real Venetian fleet lost in a storm at* **Psara, 17–18 March 1648** *(17 galleys, Grimani drowned), twenty-one years earlier.* [The whole story is on /seget/.](/seget/)
Zorzi de Franceschi goes from Candia to Zante
and from Zante to Sebenico, drawing a Venetian war pension
Marc'Antonio buys the estate; 1724 on the portal, 1732 on the cistern
ends: The town the Seget estate belongs to, the parish church with the arms on a canvas of 1650, and the family tomb with its ironwork dated 1890.
Verteneglio. The second of the western-Istrian holdings, and part of the same estate world as Seget.
Capodistria — where a Venetian war pension out of Crete was ordered to be drawn in 1730, «probably because the family was already living at Seghetto».

lanes.label: Vodnjan — five generations, read by eye
lanes.statusNote: five generations read by eye · origin not found

nodes.why: Named only in his son's patronymic — «Gio. Maria De Franceschi fu Pietro». The oldest man in the line, standing behind a marriage of the 1770s

nodes: × Michiela Zambaletta fu Cristoforo. Both dead by 1830, and neither appears in any baptism register on any film this archive can reach
Born about 1776; widower of Veniera Francin, remarries Lorenza Tesser on 30 March 1818 — the first entry this archive found in the book
Born about 1799; marries Lucia Bonassin on 9 June 1821, and the entry names his father, grandfather and great-grandfather
The other household: Giuseppe × Lucia Tromba, parents of Don Stefano the priest, Pietro the ploughman, Cristoforo the weaver and Maria Francesca
ends: Kaštelir, Vižinada, Šterna, Tar and Draguč — five parishes in the country behind Poreč and Buje, carrying the name between them on about sixty entries across the register and the roster, with Kaštelir the densest at twenty-seven. No lane on this chart runs through any of them. It is the largest piece of Istria the archive can document and cannot yet explain.

«Ob.to di Matt.o de Franceschi da Dignano», buried at Rovinj on 27 December 1728 — and in the 1840s Bona Defranceschi, daughter of Dominicus and Oliva Dorligurro, marrying there. The town-name is written down only from outside the town.
A wedding at Sissano in January 1824 witnessed by «Pietro De Franceschi di Gio., da Dignano, Tessitore».
«Ant.o De Franceschi fu Vittorio» witnessing at a wedding held by the archpriest at Sanvicenti in 1826. Recorded as a coincidence of the page and not claimed as a link.

lanes.label: Out of Corsica — never in Istria
nodes: Pietro Franceschi, 29 June 1694 – 12 February 1771, the first generation on Cap Corse
Simone Franceschi, born and dead at Ersa, 1826–1907; married Caroline Mattei
ends: Where Napoleón Franceschi's own history takes the Cap Corse family. Not ours, and the page says so.
The Danish West Indies leg of the Corsican trading diaspora.
The same movement again — Cap Corse to the Caribbean, by sea and by trade.
Where the Corsican line ends up, and where its own historian wrote it down. No contact with Istria at any point.

pens.note: Real, documented households of the name that belong to no lane yet. Each is here because the archive has read it and cannot honestly join it to one of the families above: a household moves out of this pen when a document names both ends of the join, and not before.
items: The largest town in the rebuilt record sweep (206 records, 1620–1910, across six spellings of the surname), and it was hidden in plain sight: the index writes this one city under three different names — «Fiume» (52 records), «Vitipolis» (45) and «Rijeka» (9). Vitipolis is Latin for the city of Saint Vitus, after «Terra Fluminis Sancti Viti», the river of St Vitus whose cathedral stands there. 106 records in all under those three names, 22 of them accepted — though 65 are spelt Francetich and only 20 Defranceschi, so most of the pile is a Croatian surname that may be nobody's. Kobler found three separate stocks in the civic registers and refused to join them to one another. One — Valentino, «venuto dalla Carnia», a citizen in 1739 — is almost certainly the Carnian family. The other two are not placed. Read on the register, 20 September 2026, and one of the three is no longer a guess. Valentino's marriage entry of 28 February 1737 calls him «D.num Valentinum de Franceschi ex Carnia» in the clerk's own hand — two years before the citizenship, and no longer only Kobler's word. A second household then surfaced on the same film: Joannes Baptista × Magdalena, whose son Josephus Aloysius, born 24 May 1748, is almost certainly the Giuseppe who heads the Rijeka chain. That is the household the dotted line points at, because Kobler's correspondent claimed a *«Giovanni Batt. De Franceschi venuto dalla Contea di Pisino… intorno al 1740»* for the Gologorica family — this archive's own. *The bridge is drawn dotted because nothing joins them yet: the test is Magdalena's maiden name, and it is in the County of Pazin's books, not Fiume's.*

**⭐⭐ 1825 CONFIRMS THE NIL FROM A SECOND DIRECTION.** *Slaven Bertoša's study of the Pula confirmation lists of October 1825 (Državni arhiv u Pazinu,* «Elenco Cresimati» *245) prints the surnames village by village.* **Medulin's seventeen are** *Cukon, De Marin, Garbin, Gasparin, Grakalić, Jukopila, Kirac, Lavrić, Lazarić, Lorencin, Marinović, Mihaljević, Misdaris, Privrat, Radošević, Rakić, Vojnić —* ***every one of them a name read off the Medulin death register, and no Defranceschi among them.*** *A register and a confirmation roll, independently, say the same thing.*

**⚠ But the same lists put the name four kilometres away:** «De Franceschi» *stands at* **Premantura** *and at* **Fažana** *in 1825 — both already stops on [the southern-Istrian lane](/liznjan/).*

**⚠ A LEAD, NOT A FACT, on why Medulin's registers read the way they do.** *A 2025 article claims Morlach families were transported from Dalmatia to* «**Orcevano near Medulin**» *in* **1612**. *If true it would explain the solid wall of Croatian patronymics in the books below — a planted population.* ***It gives no archival reference, its onomastics are speculative, and it misplaces Zeta.*** *To be verified in the Provincial Archive of Istria before it is believed.*

**⭐⭐⭐ AND A SECOND, A WOMAN.** *Page 33, 16 November 1873:* «**Maria (Defranceschi) Ant. Verinic uxor**», *aged* **78** — ***a Defranceschi daughter married into Medulin***, *born about 1795. The brackets are the scribe's maiden-name convention and the next line proves it:* «Maria (Vrinic q. Nic.) vid. Georgii Lorenzin». **So the name reached Medulin by marriage even though no Defranceschi household stands in the parish's own books** — *which is the [daughters' villages](/lines/) pattern already tracked at Krbune, Galižana and Labin.* ***Three Defranceschi of one generation now stand around these two villages: the Ližnjan groom of 1815 (b. ~1794), the soldier who died here in 1833 (b. ~1793), and Maria (b. ~1795).***

**⭐⭐⭐ 12 OCTOBER, LATER STILL — THE NAME IS IN A MEDULIN REGISTER AFTER ALL.** *The deaths book* «Liber Defunctorum» *(HDA inv. br. 158), page 12, year 1833, entry 43:* «**Mathæus Defranceschi q. Ant. fil. miles**» — *son of a dead Antonio, a* **soldier** — *died* **19 December 1833**, *aged* **40**, *of* «chronicus morb[us]». ***Forty in December 1833 means born about 1793, which is the year the family tree already carried for him.*** *A man this archive held as* **tree-only, with no document behind him**, *is now in a register.*

**⚠ It is a VERIFICATION, not a discovery, and the difference matters.** *His roster row already carried the ark* `3:1:3QS7-L99X-KCP6` — ***the very frame the entry is on***. *The lead was in this archive's own data and nobody had opened it.*

**⚠⚠ HE IS NOT THE LIŽNJAN MAN.** *The* «deto Marulin» *groom of 1815 was still alive to be buried at Ližnjan in* **1839**, *an* agricola; *this man was dead by December 1833, and a* soldier. ***Two Mattheuses, each son of an Antonio, four kilometres apart, both dying at forty, six years apart — the exact shape of a false join, and it is refused.***

⭐⭐ **MEDULIN — raised by David on 12 October 2026, and the archive cannot yet answer it.** *Medolino is Medulin, five kilometres down the cape from Ližnjan.* **Two things point there and neither is proof.** *First, the only two people this roster places at Medulin are* **tree-only** — «Mattheus Defranceschi b. 1793 d. 1833» *and* «Antonio Defranceschi b. 1819» — ***and those dates are the Ližnjan founders***: *the 1815 groom was 21, so born about 1794, and the baptism book has an Antonio born 15 September 1819. The tree says Medulin; the registers say Ližnjan; nobody has opened a Medulin register to adjudicate.* **Second**, *the 1861 Ližnjan marriage of Antonius Defranceski gives his bride as* «Fosca nata Lazarić … **nata e Medolino**» — *so traffic between the two parishes is proved, in that direction at least.*

**✔ 12 OCTOBER, LATER THE SAME DAY — THE OLDEST OF THE FOUR BOOKS IS NOW READ END TO END, AND THE NAME IS NOT IN IT.** *All 24 frames of* «Rođenih 1648–1649, vjenčanih 1666–1704» *(waypoint* `9R29-T3D`, *Arhiv JAZU* **Sign. VIII-158**, *film roll 24 item 2) rendered at native resolution and looked at.* ***Not one Defranceschi.*** *What is there instead is the finding:* **Medulin in these years is a village of Croatian patronymics and nothing else** — *Radonovich, Micaglievich, Gracalich, Grubisich, Golemovich, Stefanelich, Marinovich, Surionich and thirty more. The only Italian names in the whole book are the clergy and one gentleman godfather.* ***There is no Italian-surnamed household at Medulin at all between 1666 and 1705.***

**⭐⭐ But the book settles the place-name, in the parish's own hand.** «**D. Pietro Binussi Piev.o di MEDULINO**» — *the incumbent styling his own cure* — *and* «**Io Piero, Pre di MEDOLIN**», *23 November 1666.* ***Medolino is Medulin, and that is now the parish's own word for it, not an inference.***

**⭐⭐ And Ližnjan is all over this book from 1666 — ten times.** *Godparents* «da Lisigna», *a bride married in from Ližnjan in 1671, and* **«Io Pre Ant.o de Lorenzin, PIEV. DI LISIGNAN» officiating a marriage recorded in the MEDULIN book on 9 October 1666.** *The two parishes' priests served each other's altars.* ***Traffic between these two villages is not a hypothesis; it is a documented habit a hundred and fifty years before the 1815 marriage.*** *And* **Lazarich** — *the 1861 bride's own surname —* *stands here as a Medulin family in 1701 and 1705.*

**⚠ Two openings were NOT read: frames 21 and 22 carry GLAGOLITIC pages**, *and this archive cannot read the script. They are unread, not nil.* **⚠ And Medulin's births begin only in 1801**, *so a man born about 1794 is in no surviving Medulin birth register — which is the structural point below, unchanged.*

**⚠ The FamilySearch index puts only FOUR records of the name in Medulin's four books** — *which is evidence of very little, because the index demonstrably misses entries the page carries, and this archive's own harvest of it was cut short by a rate limit on exactly the field married-out daughters live in. One of the four names a* «**Tomas Defranceschi**» *who appears nowhere else here.*

**⚠ Why it matters structurally:** *Ližnjan's books begin in* **1815** *and the first Defranceschi in them is a twenty-one-year-old marrying in —* ***those volumes cannot say where he came from***. *Medulin's* **marriages run 1666–1704** *(waypoint* `9R29-T3D`, *24 frames), which is the only register in reach that predates the question. Its births start only in 1801, so a man born about 1794 is not in them. **All four of Medulin's books — 193 frames — have since been read end to end by this archive (two Glagolitic openings in the oldest excepted).**

No longer a scatter. Read by image rather than by place text, Vižinada, Kaštelir and Tar hold the same people: Giulio De Franceschi × Maria Ceselin, whose son Francesco Napoleone is baptised at Vižinada in 1818 and buried from Kaštelir's register decades later, and Angelus × Lucia-Antonia Rodella, whose son Julius is baptised at Kaštelir in January 1866 and buried at Tar in March 1870, aged four. One family across three parishes, joined by name and date rather than by any document naming two of them at once — so it is still off every lane, but it is no longer unexplained.

Fifty-six records, and until today no page at all. The city parish and Pile outside the western gate carry more of the name than any Dalmatian place but Omiš, and not one of those records writes «Dubrovnik» in its place field — they were found through the films their images sit on. A Marietta Defranceschi, daughter of a Pietro, marries a Matteo Persich and baptises children in the city in 1863 and 1871. Ragusa was a separate republic with its own patriciate; nothing joins this to the Venetian line at Zadar and Omiš, and it will not be joined on the strength of a shared surname.

Krbune, Medulin, Galižana, Labin — four parishes that hold no De Franceschi child at all, only De Franceschi mothers. (Pomer left this list on 14 October 2026: its books hold a Defranceschi household of their own, and Lucia, who married Matthaeus Lazar there, is that household’s daughter — nine children 1866–1884, six dead young.) Mariana × Vincentius Marziol at Krbune, in the County of Pazin. Dominica × Antonius Zustovich at Labin, five children 1853–1866. Catharina × Antonio Micoli at Barban — and the same couple at Vižinada eight years earlier. The surname keeps its sons and loses its daughters; these are the villages it lost them to.

A hill parish above Buzet holding two burials and nothing else: Zuane Franceschi in 1759, son of Gio Batta Franceschi, and Sebastiano De Franceschi, born and buried on 6 August 1783, son of Gio Battista De Franceschi. Twenty-four years and one Christian name apart — a father twice bereaved, or a grandfather's name coming round again. Sovinjak is not one of the parishes in the filmed collection this archive has walked, so the question stands open on the page rather than closed in a book. (Draguč, named alongside it here yesterday as equally unfilmed, is filmed — three volumes — and holds none of the name at all.)

Twelve people, one household across three generations, from before 1772 to a death in 1819 — Dominus Giovanni Battista son of Dominus Francesco, styled Dominus, a citizen-class family. Nothing on the page ties them to Gologorica, to Gračišće, or to Kobler's Fiume stocks, and this archive will not join a fourth household to them on the strength of two common Christian names.

The earliest dated Istrian record this archive holds — «morì ser Piero di Franceschi da Pola», 27 May 1619 — plus a Rovinj household across three generations from Giacomo to Piero Anto in 1736. Neither is joined to any lane. It is also where Carlo De Franceschi was married at his own bedside in 1852.

pens.head: Pomer — a household of its own, not yet placed on any line
pens.note: Pomer left the daughters' villages on 14 October 2026: its books hold a Defranceschi household of their own, read end to end on 13 and 14 October. Where the first household came from before Pomer is not found, and the second household there (a labourer out of Ližnjan, 1886) is not joined to it.
items: A Defranceschi household at house 5 from 1843: a farmer, his wife and three children, a daughter's nine grandchildren, and a widow who was the village midwife. The books (births 1816–1900, marriages 1837–1865 and 1885–1910, deaths 1842–1911) were read end to end, and the result is a household, not a name.

pens.note: A different stock of a very common name — the commonest patronymic in Italy. Kept apart on purpose: nothing joins these to Istria, and the surname alone is not a join.
items: The largest cluster of the surname anywhere — Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, São Paulo. Veneto and Trentino, not Istrian: the in-law names are Marcato, Busatto, Poletta, Raminelli, Barbiero, Negri, Catteri, Facco.
Italian-speaking Switzerland, over the border from Lombardy. A different stock of the same ordinary patronymic.
Domme De Franceski, born in Italy 1880, at the Penn Iron Mining Company at Norway, Michigan, with a wife born in Switzerland. Nothing joins him to Istria.

pens.head: Telve and the Trentino stock — kept apart, and counted
pens.note: People of the name in the Valsugana and South Tyrol (Telve, Laives, Strigno, Fiera di Primiero, Trento). They come out of David's family tree and no register has been read for them. Defranceschi is a common Trentino surname formed independently from the same patronymic; no descent connects them to the Istrian or Carnian families, and that is a working assumption, not a finding.
items: The largest single concentration of the name outside Istria and Dalmatia in this archive's roster, at Telve in the Valsugana (births 1856–1911, every one spelt Defranceschi), with Laives in South Tyrol, Strigno, Fiera di Primiero and Trento. Written down because they are there, and not claimed as relatives.

title: Seven families of one surname, and the road each of them took
caption: The teal river is the one this archive descends from, and the only one that arrived on foot looking for work. The green river at the foot is drawn dashed because it never came to Istria at all — a fully documented family of the same name that goes from Cap Corse to the Caribbean, put here so that a Franceschi found in Puerto Rico or Caracas can be seen for what they are. A dotted end-point means the attachment is family lore, not a document — Argentina hangs off Carnia only on the word of a reunion album, and Monheim is a pin on a map. A dotted curve drawn across the picture is a candidate join, on evidence short of a document, and the ones drawn are Kobler’s Giovanni Battista reaching Fiume from the County of Pazin, Ližnjan reaching Medulin down the road, and the Carnian godparents standing at Svetvinčenat. Under the rule, directly below the line this archive descends from, are the households it will not pretend to have placed: real, documented households of the name that belong to nobody yet — Rijeka, Medulin, Kaštelir and Tar, Dubrovnik, the daughters’ villages, Sovinjak, Bakar and Rovinj — with Pomer, whose household was read end to end in October, beside them. Telve and the Trentino stock, then Brazil, Ticino and Michigan, below them again, are somebody else’s entirely.

bridges.label: Kobler's Giovanni Battista — Contea di Pisino to Fiume, «intorno al 1740»
Medulin — the tree's Medulin man is a different Mattheus (a false join, refused); the traffic between the two parishes is documented
The 1660s godparent circle is Carnian, and Kandler lists Carnian families settled at Sanvincenti — company kept, not a document of arrival
